title: A Letter for the Cipher
premise: Quentin Ashgrove is hired by a dying woman, Vera Lune, to prove that her brother's murder — officially solved and closed twelve years ago — never happened. Following the money and the memories, Quentin discovers the convicted killer died in prison innocent, the body was never identified, and Vera herself may not exist in any record before 2013. As Quentin's photographic memory begins returning fragments he never consciously filed, he realizes he witnessed something that night twelve years ago and was paid to forget it. The murder hasn't happened yet because it is about to happen again: the true killer, now a city councilman, is erasing the last witnesses, and Quentin must choose between closing the case cleanly or burning his own reputation to expose a conspiracy built on his own compromised memory.
about_author: Kestrel Delacroix is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent nine years reading other people's misfortunes in triplicate before turning to fiction. They write mysteries from a houseboat on the River Medway, where they keep meticulous notes on everything except their own past.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. A frail woman named Vera Lune walks into Ashgrove Investigations with an envelope of cash and one impossible request: prove her brother's murder never happened. Quentin, intrigued by the logical paradox, accepts against his better judgment. The emotional beat is wary curiosity — a man who trusts files more than people meets a client who exists only as a signature.

chapters.title: The Closed File
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. He pulls the official record: Thomas Lune murdered in 2012, killer convicted, case closed, convict dead of illness in prison. Every document is pristine — too pristine. Quentin notices the coroner's report uses paper stock discontinued a year after the murder date. The beat is the first crack of doubt: someone rebuilt the past, and rebuilt it well.

chapters.title: A Woman Without a Shadow
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. Digging into Vera, Quentin finds no birth certificate, no tax history, nothing before 2013. His assistant Marisol, the closest thing he has to family, warns him the client is a ghost. But when Quentin visits Vera's listed address, neighbors describe her vividly — and contradict each other perfectly. The beat is unease deepening into obsession.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin, with a brief italicized memory fragment. At the original crime scene by the river, Quentin's photographic memory betrays him: images surface he never knew he had — a blue raincoat, a man's laugh, a child's shoe. He realizes he was near the scene twelve years ago. The beat is vertigo; the archive in his head has rooms he never entered.

chapters.title: The Councilman's Smile
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. The lead investigator from the old case, now retired, lets slip that Councilman Aldous Wren pushed the conviction through fast. When Quentin requests the interview records, they've been destroyed in a 'flood.' That night his office is broken into — nothing stolen but his copy of the file. The beat is the shift from mystery to menace.

chapters.title: Marisol's Doubt
chapters.summary: POV: Marisol. Seeing Quentin unravel, chasing ghosts and reciting twelve-year-old details, Marisol confronts him: is he investigating the case, or reliving it? She reveals she found a photo of young Quentin at the memorial service for Thomas Lune — a boy holding a woman's hand. The beat is found family strained by fear; loyalty versus self-preservation.

chapters.title: Vera Confesses Everything
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. Vera admits she is Thomas's widow, presumed dead, living under a new identity since she testified falsely under pressure from Wren. Her dying wish is to unmake her lie. But when Quentin cross-checks her testimony against his surfacing memories, one detail doesn't fit — she described a raincoat she couldn't have seen. The beat is betrayal braided with pity.

chapters.title: The Witness Was Me
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. The full memory returns: twelve-year-old Quentin, delivering papers, saw the real killing — and Wren's men paid his guardian to keep him quiet, dosing him until the memory sank below recall. He wasn't hired to solve the case; he was chosen because he was its loose end. The beat is devastating recognition: the cipher in the letter is himself.

chapters.title: Everything Burns Cleanly
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin and alternating Marisol. Wren moves to have Vera silenced for good; Quentin races to recover the original coroner's stock records and a surviving lab technician's sworn statement. In a tense confrontation at the council archives, Marisol records Wren implicating himself while Quentin stalls him with his perfect recall of every lie Wren has told. The beat is the climax: memory as weapon.

chapters.title: A Letter, Finally Delivered
chapters.summary: POV: Quentin. Wren falls; the conviction is vacated posthumously; Vera, spared, chooses to testify under her real name even at cost. Quentin closes the file — the first case he closes by opening it. With Marisol, he visits Thomas's grave and finally remembers his own childhood without flinching. The beat is quiet resolution: truth recovered, family chosen, memory reclaimed.
